title: Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite company's legacy code
content:
Cisco gives 27-year-old engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite 98% of the company's legacy code in 24 months — president plucks former startup founder, telling him to 'go nuts'
Cisco's president is betting on Gen Z to change the company
In a world where youth unemployment is growing as AI replaces more and more entry-level jobs, Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel is going for a different approach. According to a report by Fortune, he's given a 27-year-old ex-startup founder — brought into the company by an earlier acquisition, and previously languishing in a role five levels below — a new job to refactor 98% of the company's legacy code within 24 months.
The employee, Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, joined Cisco after it acquired EzDubs, a translation startup that Krishnamurthy helped build in 2023. While having executive experience, Patel found that "Paddy" was left "buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic."
According to the report, Patel spoke to Krishnamurthy in Cisco's office in San Francisco, where Krishnamurthy told him that he could rewrite Cisco's legacy code in a team of just two people, and that "even the most AI-forward people on [Patel's] own team weren't thinking that way."
As a result, he's now been tasked with rewriting 98% of Cisco's legacy code within 24 months, with four weeks as a proof of concept. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," according to Patel, telling him "you can go nuts."
AI coding has skyrocketed in recent months, with GitHub forced to deploy 4 million extra CPU cores and 160 petabytes of storage to cope. However, the practice is not without its pitfalls, with rogue AI agents notorious for taking unsolicited actions including deleting entire company databases, TV show edits, and production setups.
Patel hopes that there are more young hires in the Krishnamurthy mould that he can find, both in the company and externally to hire. He's looking for hires to "challenge the system and the status quo," to be "an energizer bunny that just goes and kind of revs everyone up."
Patel believes that current corporate structures work against this kind of thinking. "If you don't hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?"

He acknowledges that this will create friction, putting Gen Z employees among decades-old employees. "Tension is good.... I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don't want to have friction with the people and personalities."
Patel believes that a combination of experienced, scale operators at Cisco, alongside external hires and "entrepreneurial founders, CEOs and engineers who are AI-native" will bring results. "Either of these groups by themselves aren't nearly as potent as when all three work together. It's what creates magic."

report.summary: Cisco has tasked a 27-year-old ex-founder with using unlimited AI tokens to refactor 98% of its legacy code in 24 months.
report.background: Legacy modernization is a chronic cost center for large tech vendors: decades-old code is hard to staff, risky to touch, and expensive to maintain. Cisco's networking software, including IOS and security products, runs critical infrastructure, so rewrites carry high reliability stakes. At the same time, AI coding assistants have moved from autocomplete to agentic refactoring, prompting enterprises to test whether token-heavy AI workflows can compress multiyear projects. Cisco's move also reflects a talent debate: as AI threatens entry-level jobs, some executives want AI-native young hires to challenge entrenched processes. Patel's bet combines a former startup founder with Cisco's scale operators, but the article and reader comments highlight the gap between generating code and validating it across thousands of products.
key_points: Cisco president Jeetu Patel gave 27-year-old Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy unlimited AI tokens and a 24-month mandate to rewrite 98% of Cisco's legacy code. Krishnamurthy, who joined via Cisco's EzDubs acquisition, pitched a two-person team and got a four-week proof of concept. Patel told him to 'go nuts,' making the project an unusually public bet on AI-driven refactoring.

Krishnamurthy had been buried five levels below in an unstrategic role despite founding experience. Patel wants more hires like him: AI-native founders and engineers who challenge the status quo and energize teams. Cisco plans to blend these outsiders with experienced scale operators, accepting friction between Gen Z hires and long-tenured staff as a source of fresh ideas.

The project lands amid a surge in AI coding adoption; GitHub reportedly added 4 million CPU cores and 160 petabytes of storage to handle demand. But agentic coding carries operational risk—rogue agents have deleted databases and disrupted production. Rewriting code is only part of the job: testing, regression fixing, and certifying critical networking software could stretch far beyond 24 months.

Reader reaction underscores skepticism. Commenters question whether a translation-startup founder can safely refactor routers, switches, and firewalls that underpin the internet, and argue Cisco should start with a lower-stakes product segment. Others note intellectual-property and liability questions around AI-generated code. The debate captures the tension between AI speed and the reliability demands of infrastructure software.
report.impact: Cisco's experiment could become a template for enterprises weighing AI-led legacy modernization. If it works, expect more 'unlimited token' mandates, AI-native hires given outsized scope, and pressure on vendors to offer refactoring agents with strong test and verification loops. For developers, the premium shifts from writing boilerplate to reviewing, testing, and securing AI-generated changes; junior engineers may face both fewer entry roles and new AI-operator roles. For regular users, the stakes are reliability and security of networking gear. A high-profile failure would slow enterprise AI coding adoption; a success would accelerate it while raising questions about accountability for AI-generated code.
report.tools: Watch AI coding agents such as GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code, and Aider; agent frameworks like OpenHands and SWE-agent; and code-quality guardrails including Semgrep, CodeQL, and automated test-generation tools. For legacy refactoring, pair agents with strong CI, static analysis, and dependency/security scanning rather than relying on token volume alone.
